utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you told the Prosecution that you accepted the fact that you would have to testify but that you weren't too happy about that because the accused in that case were your former war comrades.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, I asked you whether by that you also meant Obrenovic, and you said, "Don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know, at the time I had information and I still don't know whether Obrenovic was -- what was his status at the time, whether any proceedings had been instituted against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try and refresh your memory now. You were also asked a question -- I can even show you a document, 1D202, and maybe it will be easier for you if you can read it. It's on page 2, paragraph 3. And in the English version, it's page 1, last paragraph. This is where it begins. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph reads, "Acimovic was asked whether he thought that Obrenovic tried to avoid him when he tried to contact him ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "... on the night in July 1995 when Acimovic received an order to take a firing squad to the school in Rocevici."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then you said that you didn't know what Obrenovic had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a wrong translation. I said on that occasion -- I apologise. Can you please repeat your question once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can read it for yourself but, okay. "Acimovic was asked whether he thought that Obrenovic was trying to avoid him when he tried to get in touch with him (on the night in July 1995 when Acimovic received an order to take a firing squad to the school Rocevic). Acimovic said that he didn't know what Obrenovic had in mind at the time."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was asked the following question: Whether Obrenovic knew, and I said that I supposed that he did know. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, this is a mistake, probably a wrong translation or the understanding of your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably wrong translation. I said that I supposed that Obrenovic had known. I cannot confirm whether he did or didn't, that I assume that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the following -- at the next paragraph. "Asked again whether he thought that Obrenovic was trying to avoid him, Acimovic said it wasn't logical for Obrenovic not to have known what was going on since there were army telephones, civilian telephones, radio communications, and if all this was -- all this failed, it was possible to communicate through a courier."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And it was impossible for him not to know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what my supposition was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you go on reading? Can you see that a similar question was put to you again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you answer the question. Before you start.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not clear where the questions are here. He's having him read parts of the statement and then just having him read more parts. So, so far there hasn't been a question about what this means or he's just reading, having the witness read parts of the information report and then not asking questions so I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The previous question, basically, I think you have it clear there, what was meant. The proposition was put to the witness relating to part of his interview. He was asked whether he stands by that or whether it's -- and he's even suggested that there could be a case of wrong translation. So I think we can proceed. Go ahead. I do understand what you said. I don't minimise it but I think it's better if we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As we read on, you will see that a question was put to you again whether you were under the impression that Obrenovic wanted to avoid you because he didn't answer your question. "And it was said to Acimovic that he didn't have an opinion of that question, that he should have stated that," and then you stated that you didn't know what Obrenovic thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is very ambiguous. You will agree with me, won't you? And I believe that this is just a matter of mistranslation or bad translation. As far as I can remember, I was asked, as you have just said it, and I said that I assumed that Obrenovic had known and I provided similar answers to all of these questions, and here this is represented within another context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a case of moving to your next area of questions because this has been beaten enough, I think. He's answered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, your status was changed and you were told that you were no longer a witness but a suspect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were talking about a debriefing in the brigade, in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a word that I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're right. This is a meeting. This -- our word for debriefing would be meeting or -- back or reporting back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't that an occasion to convey to your commander what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I had an opportunity to talk to the commander about that topic at the time. This was post festum, after all the developments that had taken place in our area of responsibility relative to the passage of enemy soldiers, you know that there were a lot of displaced soldiers and wounded and I believe that this meeting was focused around that, around those developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say these meetings, these debriefings, would that be an opportunity for you to say what had happened in your unit? Would that be an opportunity for you to inform the commander about what had happened in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It largely depended on the type of meeting. In any case, reporting back is an occasion to report about the tasks that had been put by the commander. We have to report back about the tasks that the commander had given to his subordinate officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are very categorical when you said that the prisoners in the school in Rocevic were not guarded by the Zvornik Brigade members and I have the same information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you also said that they were guarded by some guards from Bratunac and Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that they were guarded by guards from Bratunac and Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That you heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard, rumour had it, that that was the case but I also told you that that information was not reliable, that it was not from a reliable source.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you told that it was the first time when you had gotten in touch with the Obrenovic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, your status of witness had been reinstated. If you wish, you can look at the end of your statement, that's page 3, the last two or three paragraphs on that page. Very brief paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that true? I have not been quoting from the statement, I have put to you a question and I am asking whether what I put to you is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but here, this is not very clearly described.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said to the Obrenovic Defence team, to his lawyers, the same thing I said to the Prosecutor's Office. I answered some questions in the exact same way. They were interested in some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were interested in the details that had to do with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That will be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Who wishes to go next? Mr. Bourgon? We'll have to break at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, maybe we could take the break now and go right up till the end instead of doing it in two parts. It's already 20 after 5.00, with the break, and then we can do one session until the end, which would be better for me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are all in agreement with that. The break will be of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed, Mr. Bourgon. I'm informed that Mr. Ostojic would like to address the Chamber on some issue at the end of the sitting so please allow five minutes for that purpose. Would five minutes be enough, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Should be more than enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So five minutes before the end. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't finish today, you continue tomorrow. There is no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My name is Stephane Bourgon and I represent the accused Drago Nikolic in this case. But I take it that's not something that you were not aware of, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned to you when we met, I have a bit of a different angle of approach to the cross-examination, which will be divided into two parts. The first part I'd like to discuss with you basically your knowledge of Drago Nikolic and in the second part to go into some of the operating procedures within your battalion. Before I do so, I just have a few questions and I'll simply begin by saying or asking you to confirm that you are a battalion commander since November of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So by July of 1995, you had been a battalion commander for more than three years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it, and it is my understanding, that by 1995, you knew your job pretty well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to speak about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then let me just ask you very straightforward: Did you know your job as a battalion commander in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that many soldiers in your battalion, that the same cannot be said of them because many of these soldiers had little, and in any event, less military experience than you had? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General military knowledge and maybe I can use the expression that in many respects some of the soldiers within the Zvornik Brigade were either civilians in uniform or weekend warriors. Would that be a description of the quality of soldiers in general within Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you talking generally about the whole period or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In general. I'm just saying, let's say in 1995, the war is about to end, I'm just saying that the soldiers within Zvornik Brigade, we cannot speak, even by 1995, of a professional army; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not a professional army. That's true. But they knew what they were doing and what they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if they knew what they were supposed to do, that was because they had, indeed, some good officers, and I'm -- refer to you despite your relatively few years of service, within three years you had managed to build an effective battalion. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did my best to carry out my duties to the best of my ability, throughout the whole period that we are talking about. I said earlier that I had absolutely no military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it was a steep learning curve for you to reach the level at which you were in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see any steep curve.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I am just trying here to establish your manner of commanding in July of 1995, and all I'm trying to refer to is the fact that within the period of three years or a little more, you went from a private to a battalion commander, and you exercised command over a large number of individuals, and that is an accomplishment in itself. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not talk about any successes as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take it from another point of view. Despite the fact that war is something that nobody likes, your position as battalion commander is something that suited you well; is that correct? You felt comfortable in that position; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. What are you trying to get from me? Can you be more specific, please? I must tell you, though, I have to answer you by saying that I don't think that any single soldier can feel comfortable during the war. I really don't understand where you got that notion from. A war is the worst thing that can happen to any one people and it's therefore very hard to talk about comfort or people being suited to a role or feeling comfortable in a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's -- Mr. Acimovic, let's take a practical example so that we try to establish contact together. You remember The Untouchables, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The intervention unit, The Untouchables, do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's not an intervention unit that you put together within 2nd Battalion, The Untouchables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, tomorrow I'll show you -- I'm just mentioning where I took this from and then tomorrow I'll show you the source because I just wanted to share that with you. It wasn't my intent to contradict you with that but we have a Drinski magazine article that talks about you and the accomplishments of the Untouchables. Are you saying you have no idea who that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid you did not read the article properly. It was not The Untouchables but The Unbreakables. That was the name of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Precisely, I was going to suggest, because in the back of my mind I had the suspicion that the word was being translated into something which you wouldn't understand. So if we can make sure you're using both of you the same word in Serbo-Croat or whatever language it is. If you can read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Maybe I'll cite it for tomorrow not to waste any time because I have in the English translation The Untouchables, but I guess we are talking about The Unbreakables. So you know The Unbreakables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, these are two different words, aren't they? The Untouchables, The Unbreakables, two different things, do not belong to the same context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the original word used in the article, if you have it in the original language?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't presently, Mr. President. I just have the English translation, but I'm told that the original word is "unbreakable". It should read,"unbreakable" but what I have says "untouchable".

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, did you set up that unit, Mr. Acimovic, The Unbreakables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. An intervention platoon. That was an intervention platoon. Every infantry battalion, on the order of the brigade commander, had to establish such a platoon within the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that in March of 1995, maybe you don't remember March, but that you were visited at some point by the Drinski magazine reporter and they went to visit The Unbreakables and that they made a reporting on you about this unit? You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So can you share with us what this unit was about and what it did and what made it special?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a special unit at all. It was a unit which was a platoon, a platoon of troops, and in the true sense of the word, that platoon was some sort of a reserve unit that was behind the forward lines of the defence. If a need arose to engage them in combat in the defence sector of the battalion, and the defence sector of the Zvornik Brigade, they would have been used to that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So these were the young guys, the healthy guys, and those that would be used with the tough combat missions; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At a given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Tomorrow, I'll give you the copy in your language and we can share that because this is only to establish that it's something that you, according to this paper that I have, that you took some great pride in, the creation of this unit and the fact that it was involved in difficult situations. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That unit assisted everywhere. It was used if one of our positions came under attack. This platoon and platoons similar to this one were used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. A few more personal questions and then we move on to my questions relating to Drago Nikolic. Just to confirm that your house was in the Rocevic area, that has been established already, but it was some 300 metres from the school in Rocevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 300 to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And most of the soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the crow flies, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I was going to say most of the soldiers but a fair amount of soldiers in the 2nd Battalion, they were from Rocevic, even though Rocevic was not in your battalion defence area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no single company that would be composed exclusively of natives of Rocevic but in any case, the 1st Infantry Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Company , interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- was mostly composed of troops from Rocevic but there were other troops from other villages. In the 2nd Infantry Company, we also had an infantry platoon from Rocevic, and that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the -- your knowledge of Drago Nikolic in 1995, which is the first part of my cross-examination today. Yesterday you said, and I quote from page 21, lines 22 and 23, you stated yesterday that the question was, "Did you know an officer named Drago Nikolic?" And your answer was: "Yes." "What was his position at the time?" And he was: "... assistant brigade commander for intelligence and security." Do you recall that giving that answer yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think just as a matter of just as a small correction, you would agree with me that he wasn't assistant commander for both intelligence and security, but just for security. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is it something you're not aware of or maybe you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were asked to describe the relationship, you described it as being "... a fair relationship, the relationship between me and Drago Nikolic, when it came to our cooperation and our duties, we never had any disagreements so it was a fair relationship and a correct relationship." So that's what you said yesterday, and I guess this is also your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also said that you at times socialised and you gave that information also to my colleague from the Prosecution, that at times you went out and you had drinks with Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you remember meeting with the investigator assigned to the Nikolic team? And that was quite recently, and that was, I believe, earlier in June? Do you remember meeting with our investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At their request, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. And I just want to -- because when you met him, the information he provided me with is that, in fact, the relationship between Drago and yourself was more something like and I'll quote his words - you can correct me, if that is correct or not - the witness says that he had an extraordinary relationship with Drago Nikolic, both military and personal. Sorry for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one might say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my friend is clearly cross-examining with a report of some kind from his investigator. I think we are entitled to see that and have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have information and notes, I'm not going to share my notes with my colleague. Those are notes that I got from my investigator, like we don't have access to their notes, we don't give access to our notes. It's not a statement, it's just a -- and the witness is perfectly free to confirm or not to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But he's reading from a document. I'm entitled to see what he's reading from and clearly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's telling you they are his notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They are not his notes. He's said that they are what his investigator wrote down from an interview with a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't see where my colleague is going with this. This is just information that I have. Someone is pointing to me at Rule 97 here. And that's information that I have received that is privileged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop it therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't see what the problem is. At least he should wait until it's something that's contentious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop it there, and we will have some consultations on this. It will only take us a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We consider such a document as privileged provided-- and we take your word for it -- that it is not a statement by the witness when he was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is not a statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see where the privilege is when it's a witness -- where the witness is discussing something with an investigator. Once it's written down -- of course, our investigators, when they write something down, we turn that into a report and give it to them. If we used investigator's notes in cross-examination, of course they would say, "I'd like to see what" -- if I picked up and said, "All right I'm reading from my investigator's notes," is there any way that wouldn't be shared with them during cross? Would they accept that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not going to delve into the rights and practices of the Prosecution. I'm just dealing -- we are just dealing at the moment with the issue that you raised, and Rule 70(A) specifically provides that: "Notwithstanding the provisions of Rules 66 and 67, reports, memoranda, or other internal documents prepared by a party, its assistants or representatives in connection with the investigation or preparation of the case, are not subject to disclosure or notification under those Rules."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I agree with that but when it is read out in court, to be used in cross-examination, I think that changes things. It's no longer anything internal because he's reading it to the entire world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It still remains his notes. It still remains his notes. So -- let's not waste more time on this. We are taking your word that this is not a statement but it's just notes that were prepared for you by your assistant and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear I would not want Mr. Bourgon's notes. And maybe we'll file something on this but if the investigator writes down something which a witness has told him and then that is read back to the witness, I think I have a right to see what has been written down by that investigator for completeness. When you use something in cross-examination normally the other side, whatever it is, gets to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have handed down our decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed and our ruling is to be understood to refer specifically to the document that you have and the part that you read from it, or that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Mr. Acimovic. As I've mentioned to you when we met, this is the game and they do this regularly so it's -- don't take it personally, please. I just asked you to qualify the idea of the relationship, both military and personal, between yourself and Drago Nikolic. I would like you to confirm that it is your opinion, and at least it was until that time, that Drago Nikolic was a highly professional military officer who was very strict on military rules and that he was not a big talker, he didn't speak much. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that he was strict. It is not my call to be the judge of Drago's abilities. I only said that my relationship with him was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree that he was a professional military officer that, he behaved in a professional manner, are you able to qualify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At any rate, I believe that he did his best to perform his duties in a proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, just to move immediately into those conversations that you testified you say you had with Drago Nikolic on that night and that morning, well, to begin with, you can confirm that these -- and I believe you said that already, you said it in your statement, that that conversation took place on an open line and that no codes were used for that conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that at the time you believed Drago Nikolic was transmitting an order which came from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that at any rate, this was not an order that he personally issued, that he did not order that himself but, rather, that he conveyed somebody else's order, but I repeat I only assumed that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's exactly what I'm simply asking you. And would I be correct in saying that when you -- when you tried to remember back the content of the conversation, you told to the Prosecution on a number of occasions that it is difficult to remember the exact word or details in which this conversation took place? Would you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please can you remind me of that statement of mine? I don't know which one are you referring to. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do. Let's take, for example, the -- your second interview and we can call this up on e-court, and that is at 3D154, and I'd like to have page 17 to 19 in English and in -- sorry, page 19 in English and page 20 in B/C/S. So you can look at this in your language, just to remind you what you told the Prosecution at that time. Okay. I'd like to, if we can just -- we will have the -- here. Now, I'll ask you to look, Mr. Acimovic, at page 20, lines 1 to 3 up there, where it says, "He was not pleased" -- "He was not protesting ... He was not pleased, he raised his voice at me and things like that. But I cannot remember the exact words or details in which this conversation took place." Do you remember saying that to the Prosecution in your second interview? At the top, lines 1 to 3. Were these the words that you used with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no need for me to consult this document at all. Could you please repeat your question and please be more precise? Tell me what you want me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm just saying, Mr. Acimovic, that what you told the Prosecution is simply that it is difficult, looking back, to remember precisely the exact words or details in which this conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is how the interview evolved. When --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have very limited time and I'm simply asking, is it difficult today to remember the details or do you remember every single detail? Because you said on three different occasions, and I can refer to those, but I'm just trying here to establish something that -- remember things that you said, "I cannot remember the exact words or details in which this conversation took place." Do you remember ever saying that to the Prosecution? Because you've already described that conversation in your examination-in-chief. All I want to know is did you tell the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I've told you that I can't remember every single word, every single comma. These are some details that I don't think are that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. I'll just say that -- I'll just suggest to you that it was your impression at the time that Drago Nikolic was under pressure and that he had no choice but to pass the order or whatever message he passed to you. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment when I talked to Drago, I did not feel that. However, on reflection, since I know what Drago is like, I really gave it a long and hard thought, to try and guess what could have made him put such a pressure on me, especially in light of the fact that my relationship with him had been good, as I've already told you. Also, I would like to emphasise that again I assume, but I only assume, that he did it on somebody else's orders. But I can't be sure of that. This is merely my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that he was under pressure when relaying those words to you, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim for a fact that he was under pressure. This is just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered the question. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Acimovic, would I be correct in saying that you were very surprised to see Drago Nikolic involved into any of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you think, Mr. Acimovic, that Drago Nikolic was able to issue such an order or would you agree that he had no authority or competence to be able to organise in his own any such action? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that the operation was not his own initiative, that he did it -- did not do it of his own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we discussed this when we met. Based on your knowledge of what happened, would you agree that Drago Nikolic was a small player and no more than a pawn in those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that he wasn't in a position to plan all that on his own. I only assume that he acted on somebody's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned to me when we met, Mr. Acimovic, that it was your impression that Drago Nikolic had been misused at the time. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that whoever participated in all of this was misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you elaborate with respect to Drago Nikolic? I'm just referring to our conversation. I don't want to put it to you. I just want you to repeat what you told me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This conversation took place in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on. After the phone call that you say you had with Drago Nikolic on that morning, and you said it was something around 7.00, would I be right in saying that after that you had no more dealings with Drago Nikolic concerning those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said at 7.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: After 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that morning's conversation, I wasn't in touch with Drago in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in -- at any time when you went in -- when were you in Rocevic, you never saw Drago Nikolic there; would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in response to a question from my colleague that you discussed these events with Trbic at some point. And my question is that you never discussed these events with Drago Nikolic, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the meeting which was referred to by my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic, later on in the month, you can confirm that Drago Nikolic was present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm, but I suppose he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you did not discuss these events at that time with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on to a different area of my cross-examination, and again, this is all material that we've discussed and I took it from your statements. And I would first suggest to you that keeping prisoners in the school in the village of Rocevic was a dangerous thing to do because there were no soldiers in the village and no one was armed to defend the population there. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In any case, a school is not a facility where one should keep prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I beg to disagree with you on this but that's not the issue of my question. So let's get to my question. My question is simply in that context, and you've testified at length about the context, in the military situation, and at that particular moment, to put prisoners in the school in Rocevic, in the context at the time, that was a dangerous thing to do. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the soldiers that were there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I believe you may have mentioned this -- I don't have the exact reference in your testimony but I have the reference in your first interview -- where you mentioned that soldiers in the trenches, your soldiers on the front line, they learned about Rocevic and they were ready to leave the front line, which would have been a disaster. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They heard about this woman being wounded, and about the behaviour of the soldiers who were down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it would have been a disaster had they decided to leave the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. But I don't think that that could have happened without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the -- would you agree with me that anyone in the -- in Zvornik Brigade at that time was fully aware of the difficulty of the situation on the front line at that particular moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll try and make it more precise. You yourself knew that a column was approaching and that there was a risk of attack. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received telegrams to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that anybody on the front line, all of the battalions, would be aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And such information was disseminated to the battalion by the brigade command. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that the Zvornik Brigade itself, in those circumstances, would never have instigated, planned or ordered such a risky and dangerous move of putting prisoners in the schools?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move to another segment of my cross-examination. And I just want at this time to go over with you some members of your battalion and to see where they were in July of 1995 during those events that you testified about. So if we begin by Vujo Lazarevic, he was your assistant commander for morale and religious affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on that night, he was the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it was Mitar Lazarevic. That's another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You're right to point this out because yesterday you said Vujo Lazarevic was the duty officer and today you said Mitar Lazarevic was the duty officer. I know two different persons but which one was the officer between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I think that Mitar Lazarevic was the duty officer but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the two were present, and they were on duty that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. One of them was on duty, and I said that I think that it was Mitar Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the other person, Vujo, was present. What was he doing there during the night, if he wasn't on duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We in the battalion command were billeted there as well, only one floor above. That means that the room where the duty officer was had two or three beds, where officers from the battalion command would sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's exactly the reason why I asked these questions, to allow the Trial Chamber to understand exactly how the battalion command, where it was, how it worked, and I have a couple of questions for that. But just to go back to Mitar Lazarevic, which is the second one on my list, you've already said that he was the person responsible for general affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mitar was not an officer, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of my assistants were officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the post of clerk for general affairs or person responsible for general affairs, is that a post normally held by an officer? Is that an officer post? Or is that a clerk position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An officer should hold this position, but since this was a desk officer in charge of general affairs, as you can see for yourself, we had privates discharging these duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. And Vujo, what rank was he? Vujo Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had no rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No rank. So they were both ordinary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Privates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But in occupying the roles of assistant commander with your battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I move on quickly to Stevan Savic. He was your deputy commander and he was absent from your battalion at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Milorad Sakotic he was your assistant commander for security and he was also absent in Trnovo at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that he was in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have any other information that he was anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. A group of soldiers was at the time involved in carrying out combat missions in that area but I'm not sure whether it was Trnovo or some other location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So he was away. You had sent him on some kind of mission away from the command at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's all I'm trying to get it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Zivojin Pisic, he was your quartermaster; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Assistant commander for logistics, Zivan Pisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's just a mistake with my language because I happened to be a quartermaster and assistant commander for logistics before myself. So there are moving on to this man, you changed the first name, I thought it was Zivojin but you gave me a different name, Zivan Pisic. He worked in the command with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that you had a number of radio operators working in the command also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that there was a large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, we'll go through the list just to confirm whether these people are your radio operator or communications people. Miodrag Pisic, he was one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Dragan Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Goran Ilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Milisav Cvijetinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you just at this point -- maybe we can for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, where did these people work physically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean where they were deployed or situated? Not far from the battalion command, some 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I move on to -- you had a cook with the battalion command, that was Milan Jovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were there any other persons that you may remember that I may have missed that were working in the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were probably more people there, but I'm not claiming that all that you have named here were present. Also, from those communications officers that you mentioned, I also cannot say that whether all of them were present or only some of them were present. The same also applies to the cooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was those are persons working in the command, they are assigned to the command of the 2nd Battalion, that was the only purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were members of the battalion, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have -- were there any persons for the security of the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what way? Are you referring to the military police and things like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Anybody who would ensure the physical protection of the battalion command, other than the people we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I just -- may we go into private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm just curious. You mentioned Goran Radic. Was he present in July 1995 or during these events, was he present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did he -- but I take it he did not drive you when you went to Rocevic school or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why is this so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most definitely not. It is possible that he was among the soldiers who were outside the defence area of the battalion but I'm not sure. But in many other cases, and other situations, I drove the car myself, when I went home and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Acimovic. My next section is that I would just like to discuss a bit of well, the company commanders, you've mentioned all the company commanders already but let's just confirm that and then I'll be -- I think that will be it for me for today. First company was Dragan Stjepanovic, you said that already; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mico Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And 2nd Company was Miroslav Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Risto Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the 3rd Company was Milan Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it that his deputy was Petko Tomic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm moving to a different area. I think the Trial Chamber requested five minutes. I would prefer to stop here, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. It's fine with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Acimovic, and we'll see you in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think the witness can leave the courtroom. Mr. Acimovic, same advisory as yesterday. Please no communication with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. There's two points I'd like to raise. One, today in the transcript of this witness, on page 40, line 2, and I had a discussion with my learned friend - I'm not sure if it was a translation problem or not, the witness specifically testified that he spoke to all Defence teams. And I think my learned friend will agree that, even during our discussion yesterday, the Beara Defence team did not at any time meet with this witness. And I believe my friend agrees with that, because he has inquired with this witness prior to him taking the oath with whom he met, so I just wanted that to be clarified, not to waste time. I guess he's standing and I'll just stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct. I took that as the witness saying, "I met with everybody who wanted to meet with me," and the Beara team was not amongst those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken, and it goes on record. The second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The second point was the Court's request on the progress on the aerial images. We have discussed that at length and on multiple occasions and we are coming closer. We are waiting to get some other verification from the actual source of those images, and we think we can get it to the Court, a final determination on whether we need to continue to discuss that in the next week to 10 days. But we are actually meeting on that issue and we have met on numerous occasions on that, and we seem to be getting closer on the information that we feel is required and necessary. So I just wanted to advise the Court on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The important thing is that something is being done and you haven't put it in deep freeze, in other words. Yes, Mr. McCloskey? Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Mr. President, and also on the issue of -- Mr. Vanderpuye has informed me that he has finished his proofing and is not planning on seeing the person again, though he would like to have the ability to do that, of course. And so we really, hopefully, we don't have an issue and I would like to avoid controversy if possible. However, this is an issue we feel strongly about, that these sorts of orders that are being requested are inappropriate so, perhaps some time we need to deal with it but at this point, it doesn't look like it's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I suppose you also -- it's the case of waiting for our Obrenovic decision as well, because it might give you an indication of where we stand on such issues. All right. Perhaps we will have a second verification of that tomorrow, Mr. McCloskey, and then we will ask Mr. Bourgon what position he will be taking. We'll deal with it tomorrow. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to inform the Trial Chamber, I had estimated two hours for this witness. I've already taken one hour. I will require more time tomorrow in light of the testimony. I would say probably two hours, maybe a little more but I'll try to cut it down. My aim is to finish in one session. Not sure I'll be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. We will use our discretion, of course, Mr. Bourgon, but we believe that we use it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any more estimates while we've got everybody so I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I had asked -- you were here, no? The Beara team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sometimes things change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Beara team asked for 45 minutes, probably will be less. And then we have the Pandurevic team 30 minutes at the most, between 20 and 30. The others, I don't think there is a change in position, unless I hear statements to the contrary. I see Madam Fauveau is not requiring, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Josse the same. So basically we have another two hours from Mr. Bourgon, roughly, and then Mr. Meek will kindly break the news to us tomorrow morning after a whole night of deep thinking on the subject. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 22nd day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
